title: That Morning Soda Might Be Messing With Your Brain More Than You Think
summary:
Have you ever noticed that caffeine makes you feel weird—maybe jittery or headachy—while your parents just feel more awake? Sophia Zeng, a 16-year-old student in Beijing, wondered the same thing. So she decided to investigate. Her surprising discovery? Caffeine might actually change how genes work in a young brain, and not in a good way.

Sophia started by digging through old studies on adult mice. She found clues that caffeine could switch certain genes on or off in the brain. Then she grew rat brain cells in a dish and gave them caffeine. Two days later, she looked under a microscope. The cells that got more caffeine had fewer connections, called synapses (the tiny gaps where brain cells talk to each other). It was like the caffeine was making the brain's wiring simpler and weaker.

Next, she studied young zebrafish. The fish that got caffeine swam more and acted anxious, darting into scary parts of their tank. When Sophia checked their brains, four important genes for brain growth were less active. That's like dimming the lights on a construction site—things don't get built right.

Here's the really interesting part: the gene changes in young fish were different from what she saw in adult rat cells. That suggests caffeine hits a young brain harder. Sophia thinks we should be more careful about caffeine, especially for kids. "We really don't talk about caffeine, even though we drink it," she says. Her work earned her a spot at the huge Regeneron International Science & Engineering Fair, where 1,725 students from around the world shared their discoveries.
why_it_matters: If caffeine can change the way young brains develop, then kids might want to think twice before drinking soda or energy drinks, and it's important for scientists to keep studying everyday substances to keep us healthy.

background_read: Many teens drink soda or energy drinks that contain caffeine. Scientists already know caffeine can affect sleep and make people feel jittery.
The Regeneron International Science & Engineering Fair (ISEF) is a huge global science competition where high-school students present their research.
Sophia Zeng's project on caffeine's effect on young brains was one of the entries at this fair, which brings together over a thousand young scientists from around the world.
Article_Structure: WHO: Sophia Zeng, a 16-year-old student in Beijing.
WHAT: She experimented to see how caffeine changes brain cells and genes in young animals, using rat cells and zebrafish.
WHERE: In her science lab in Beijing, growing rat brain cells in a dish and studying zebrafish in a tank.
WHY: She was curious why caffeine made her feel weird while adults just felt awake, and she wanted to find out if caffeine could be bad for developing brains.

perspectives.description: Sophia's discovery is exciting because it warns young people about hidden dangers of caffeine and could lead to healthier drinks and better advice for kids.
Others say the study used animal cells and fish, so we don't know for sure if caffeine affects human children in the same way. More research is needed before making big conclusions.
